strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: building a pretrained, zero-shot capable foundation model that fuses text, endogenous image, and time series modalities for cross-domain forecasting, going beyond existing unimodal foundation models and end-to-end multimodal supervised models.

The proposed architecture (token distillation, Modality-Guided Self-Attention with cross-modal correlation injection, Prototype-Guided Flow Matching with a learnable Period/Trend prototype bank) is reasonably well described and technically coherent, with a sensible motivation for replacing the standard Gaussian starting point of flow matching with a data-informed prototype.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS) and covering zero-shot unimodal, zero-shot/few-shot multimodal, and probabilistic forecasting settings, with consistent state-of-the-art or near-SOTA performance against 10+ strong baselines.
Ablation studies (Table 4) demonstrate that both the Modality-Guided Attention and Prototype-Guided Flow Matching contribute meaningfully and interact (cascading degradation when both removed).
Efficiency/scalability analysis (parameters, MACs, memory, inference time, and sampling-count vs. accuracy trade-off) is provided, giving practical insight into deployment cost.
Reasonably thorough documentation of pretraining corpus construction, benchmark statistics, and baseline implementations in the appendix, aiding reproducibility to some extent.
weaknesses: Potential data leakage/circularity concern in the pretraining corpus construction: the textual descriptions are generated by GPT-4 given the raw time series itself and asked to "analyze the future trend," which risks leaking future information into the text modality during pretraining; the paper does not clearly address whether the text generation process is restricted to historical context only, undermining confidence in how much of Aurora's gain stems from genuine cross-modal reasoning vs. information leakage baked into the corpus.

The few-shot (10%) vs. full-shot comparison in Table 1 is somewhat asymmetric — Aurora benefits from large-scale pretraining while baselines are trained from scratch on the target domain; while this is stated, the framing of "outperforms full-shot baselines with only 10% of data" may overstate the fairness of the comparison without deeper analysis of why this holds (e.g., is it purely thanks to pretraining scale, not multimodal fusion specifically?).

Ablation studies are limited to a single benchmark (TimeMMD multimodal zero-shot); no ablations are shown for the unimodal or probabilistic settings, nor isolated ablations of individual components such as token distillation, the learnable metric W, or the prototype bank initialization choices (trigonometric/exponential/log/polynomial bases).

Novelty of the flow-matching contribution is incremental relative to existing stochastic-interpolant/rectified-flow work that already allows non-Gaussian priors; the core idea of using informative retrieval-based initial points is a reasonable but modest extension.

The manuscript has numerous typographical and grammatical errors (e.g., "Corss-domain," "merticulously-designed," "inituitively," "scability," "hevay") that suggest insufficient proofreading and could obscure technical precision in places.

No variance/statistical significance reporting across multiple runs or seeds, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (e.g., single-digit percentage MSE reductions) are robust or within noise, especially for smaller datasets like Agriculture/Economy.

Limited discussion of failure cases, modality ablation robustness (e.g., performance degradation when only one of text/image is available at inference, beyond a brief mention of random masking during pretraining), or sensitivity to the quality/availability of externally generated text descriptions in real-world deployment.

The claim of "pioneering" multimodal time series foundation models is only lightly supported by related-work discussion; closely related concurrent works (e.g., Time-VLM, various LLM-based time series works) are used as baselines but the differentiation in framing versus truly concurrent foundation-model efforts could be more thoroughly contextualized.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: combining multimodal (text/image) knowledge with a pretrained time series foundation model to support zero-shot cross-domain forecasting, filling a gap between unimodal foundation models and end-to-end multimodal supervised models.

The proposed architecture integrates several components (modality distillation, modality-guided attention, prototype-guided flow matching) in a reasonably coherent pipeline, and the paper provides fairly extensive experiments across three benchmark suites (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS) and a large number of baselines.

Ablation studies (Table 4) and an inference-scalability study (Figure 5) are included, along with an efficiency comparison (Table 8) and full result tables in the appendix, which aids some interpretability of contributions.

The idea of using a learnable trend/period prototype bank as an alternative to Gaussian initialization for flow matching is a reasonable technical contribution that could be of independent interest for generative time-series models.
weaknesses: Potential information leakage in constructing the pretraining corpus: the sample-wise textual descriptions are generated by feeding the *entire* (including future) time series segment to GPT-4 and asking it to 'analyze the future trend,' as shown in the example prompt (Figure 7). If the resulting text encodes information about the actual future values/trend that would not be available at real-world inference time, then the multimodal guidance the model learns to rely on during pretraining is not representative of genuine domain-knowledge conditioning, undermining the central claim of the paper and casting doubt on the reported zero-shot gains.

The 'image modality' is a deterministic rendering (FFT-period based reshaping) of the same time series used as the primary temporal input; it is not an independent source of information, and the framing of this as genuine 'cross-modality' fusion providing 'geometric domain knowledge' is questionable, since VisionTS already established this transform is largely redundant with the temporal signal itself.

Novelty is primarily architectural recombination of existing components (ViT/BERT encoders, cross-attention distillation, DiT-style condition decoding, flow matching à la Lipman et al., prototype retrieval) rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle; each individual piece has clear precedent in prior work.

The writing quality is poor and contains numerous typos and grammatical errors throughout (e.g., 'Corss-domain', 'corrsponding', 'merticulously-designed', 'hevay', 'propriate', 'scability', 'trainied to tutor'), suggesting insufficient proofreading and raising concern about the overall rigor and care taken in the submission.

No statistical significance testing, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported for any experiment; given the fairly large parameter count of Aurora (418.6M, largest or near-largest among compared foundation models) and the modest margins in several tables, it is hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust or attributable to model capacity/pretraining data scale rather than the proposed architectural novelties.

Aurora has the highest per-sample inference latency among all compared methods in the efficiency table (83.5ms vs. 7.4-81.3ms for others), which is a nontrivial practical drawback for a 'foundation model' intended for out-of-box deployment, and this cost/benefit tradeoff is not adequately discussed.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is unclear: many unimodal foundation model baselines are not designed to use text/image input at all, so the 'multimodal' zero-shot comparisons in Table 1 may not be an apples-to-apples comparison of modeling capability versus simply having access to additional (LLM-synthesized) information at training time.

Reproducibility concerns: the cross-domain multimodal pretraining corpus (with LLM-generated captions) is central to the model's claimed capabilities, but there's no indication that this corpus, the generation prompts (beyond one example), or trained model weights will be released, limiting the community's ability to verify or build on the results.

Some notational/dimensional details (e.g., the correlation computation via a learnable metric W between distilled image and text tokens of the same time index, and how the described distillation numbers Kimage/Ktext interact with per-token attention) are only partially specified, making full technical verification difficult from the text alone.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap between unimodal time series foundation models (which lack explicit domain knowledge) and end-to-end multimodal supervised models (which lack zero-shot capability), by proposing a pretrained multimodal (text+image+time) foundation model.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning three well-recognized benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS) and covering unimodal/multimodal, deterministic/probabilistic, and zero-shot/few-shot settings against a large number of strong baselines (18 total).

Consistently strong empirical results with substantial margins over prior SOTA (e.g., 27-31% MSE reduction over Sundial/VisionTS on TimeMMD, 15-23% over Time-MoE/ROSE on TSFM-Bench), and even competitive zero-shot performance against full-shot supervised multimodal baselines.

Reasonably designed ablation study (Table 4) demonstrating the individual and combined contributions of the Modality-Guided Self-Attention and Prototype-Guided Flow Matching modules, showing a cascading degradation when both are removed.

The Prototype-Guided Flow Matching idea (initializing the ODE from learned period/trend prototypes conditioned on multimodal context rather than pure Gaussian noise) is a sensible and reasonably novel adaptation of flow matching for time series.
Good reproducibility support: detailed model configurations (Table 7), efficiency/latency comparisons (Table 8), baseline code repositories, and dataset statistics are all provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Potential label leakage in the pretraining corpus construction: the GPT-4-generated textual descriptions (e.g., Figure 7 example) appear to explicitly encode the numeric trajectory of the time series itself (e.g., 'started with 22.7... dropped to 2.3... to 0.1'), which risks turning the text modality into a shortcut that directly reveals target values rather than genuine independent domain knowledge; this raises concerns about whether the model's strong pretraining-derived gains reflect real cross-modal reasoning or a data-construction artifact.

There is a potential distribution mismatch between the synthetic, GPT-4-simulated pretraining text corpus and the real, human/domain-sourced text used in downstream benchmarks (e.g., TimeMMD), which is not explicitly analyzed or discussed.

Individual technical components (cross-attention-based modality fusion/guiding, distillation via learnable query tokens, DiT-style condition decoding, flow matching) are largely adaptations of existing techniques from vision-language and diffusion/flow-based literature; the overall novelty is primarily in engineering integration rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

No ablation directly isolating the contribution of each individual modality (e.g., text-only vs. image-only vs. time-only variants) is provided; the paper only ablates the fusion/attention mechanism and the flow-matching module, leaving unclear how much each modality independently contributes versus the architecture choices.

No variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are reported for the main comparisons or ablations, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported improvements, especially where margins between top methods are small (e.g., ETTm2 in Table 10).

The manuscript contains numerous typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'Corss-domain', 'merticulously', 'hevay', 'inituitively', 'corrsponding') that suggest insufficient proofreading and slightly undermine the presentation quality expected at a top-tier venue.

The comparison in the few-shot multimodal setting (Aurora trained with 10% data vs. full-shot supervised baselines) is favorable to Aurora but the framing risks overstating fairness, since Aurora also benefits from a large-scale multimodal pretraining stage that the compared end-to-end baselines do not have access to.

The cost and scalability of the LLM-based data generation pipeline used to build the multimodal pretraining corpus (e.g., GPT-4 API costs, quality control, potential hallucination in generated descriptions) is not discussed, raising reproducibility and practical-scaling concerns for the community.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: building a multimodal (text+image) time series foundation model that supports zero-shot cross-domain inference, unlike prior unimodal TSFMs or end-to-end multimodal supervised models.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 5 diverse benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS, TFB, EPF) spanning deterministic, probabilistic, unimodal, and multimodal settings, with consistently strong results against a large set of baselines (11+ foundation models and multiple end-to-end supervised models).

Technically interesting architectural contributions: Modality-Guided Multi-head Self-Attention that injects cross-modal correlation into temporal attention, and Prototype-Guided Flow Matching that replaces standard Gaussian initialization with learned period/trend prototypes as a more informative starting point for the ODE-based generative process.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (modality ablations, attention-guidance ablations, prototype bank size, sampling-number scalability, efficiency analysis) and appendix material (dataset corpus composition, prompt design for LLM-generated text, visualizations of prototypes and attention weights) that aid interpretability and partial reproducibility.
Includes efficiency/inference-cost analysis and short-term forecasting evaluation, broadening the practical relevance of the claims.
weaknesses: The Cross-Domain Multimodal Time Series Corpus's textual descriptions are synthetically generated by GPT-4 conditioned on the raw series and a domain description/report; since the 'future trend' text is generated with some knowledge of the underlying series characteristics (per the example prompts explicitly asking to 'analyze the future trend'), there is a serious risk of information leakage between the text modality and the forecasting target, which could substantially inflate reported gains and undermines the ecological validity of the multimodal pretraining signal for real-world deployment where such oracle-like text would not be available.

Reproducibility is significantly hampered: the reproducibility statement claims code/checkpoints are released but the links are blank/missing in the manuscript; hyperparameter and architecture details for baselines are only partially specified, and the LLM-driven corpus curation pipeline (quality-checking loop) is described only qualitatively.

The paper's central motivating claim (similar histories, different futures across domains) is illustrated only qualitatively via cherry-picked showcase visualizations (Appendix C.1) rather than a quantitative controlled experiment isolating this exact phenomenon, weakening the causal narrative connecting the architecture design to the claimed advantage.

Some baseline comparisons appear potentially unfair or under-specified: e.g., in Table 1, Aurora's 10% few-shot numbers are compared against full-shot multimodal baselines, and it is unclear whether these baselines were also given the same LLM-generated text used to construct Aurora's pretraining corpus or the original TimeMMD text, potentially confounding the comparison; additionally many foundation baselines are evaluated with '-' (excluded because in their own pretraining sets) which complicates uniform comparison across models.

The writing has numerous typos, inconsistent citations (e.g., EPF cited inconsistently as Olivares et al. 2023 vs Wang et al. 2024b in different sections, TTM's citation swapped with Olivares et al. in the baseline list) and grammatical errors ('Corss-domain', 'merticulously-designed', 'inituitively') that reduce clarity and suggest insufficient proofreading for a top-tier venue.

The novelty of individual components is somewhat incremental/combinatorial: cross-attention-based modality guidance, distillation via learnable query tokens, and flow matching with learned priors are each recognizable techniques from prior work (DiT, Lipman et al. flow matching, cross-attention distillation), and the paper does not clearly isolate how much of the gain stems from the novel combination versus simply using more/better pretraining data compared to baselines.

No discussion of computational cost or feasibility of obtaining high-quality domain text at inference time for real-world zero-shot deployment; the paper does not report the impact of noisy/low-quality or missing text on performance beyond ablations that swap it out with an ideal generated description, which is unlikely to reflect realistic zero-shot text quality.

Statistical significance (variance across seeds) is not reported for any experiment, making it hard to assess whether the sometimes modest MSE/MAE differences (e.g., some 1st-place counts with tiny margins) are meaningful.
